feedback: If a learner confuses the tsunami warning with the earthquake itself, or thinks there is no way to warn people, walk through the chain: undersea quake detected → sea-level sensors → alert to evacuate to high ground.
If a learner dismisses drills as obvious or pointless, have them compare evacuation times with and without a practised route, so the time saved is visible.
If a learner focuses only on the building, ask what protects people once a tsunami is already coming, steering toward warning and evacuation.
activities.intendedInsight: Reducing human impact is a system — detect, warn, act — not just a stronger wall; rehearsed evacuation and clear routes save time when seconds count, and a tsunami warning is distinct from feeling the earthquake itself — though near the coast, strong or long shaking is itself a natural warning to move to high ground without waiting for an official alert.
learnerActions: Switch to a coastal-town setting and place the pieces of a warning system: a detection buoy/sensor offshore, a warning siren, a marked evacuation route, and a high-ground or vertical-evacuation destination.
Trigger an undersea earthquake and tsunami, then run a timed evacuation and watch how quickly people reach safety.
Change one part of the system (move the route, add a siren, choose vertical evacuation) and re-run the timed evacuation to see the effect on how many reach high ground in time.

Explain in order how the system works: undersea quake detected → sea-level sensors confirm a tsunami wave (the sea may rise or first pull back) → alert reaches people → evacuate to high ground or a tall, strong building, supported by rehearsed community drills.
activities.title: Coastal town: a detect → warn → act evacuation system

feedback: If a learner cannot tell which way the tower is leaning or racking, rotate the model so the failure plane faces them before re-shaking.
If base isolation still reads as a firmer attachment, rotate to the cutaway and watch the ground slide under the lagging building.
activities.intendedInsight: Toppling, centre of mass, racking and decoupling are spatial; rotating a 3D model can make the direction of sway and the ground-building decoupling easier to see than a flat side-on view.
learnerActions: Rotate a 3D model of a built tower to view it from any angle, then apply shaking and watch it sway and collapse in depth rather than only side-on.
Compare an un-braced frame racking in three dimensions with a braced or base-isolated tower that holds its shape or decouples from the ground.
View a 3D base-isolation cutaway: watch the bearings let the ground slide beneath while the building lags behind in space (inertia).
activities.title: Rotate the tower in 3D: watch it sway, topple, and decouple

feedback: If a learner still expects a fully earthquake-proof building, have the engineer reframe the goal as protecting people and buying escape time, with damage reduced and delayed but not guaranteed to be prevented in every earthquake.
If answers stay abstract, ask the learner to tie each claim back to a specific trial from their own comparison grid.
activities.intendedInsight: Real hazard engineering is a judgement about reducing impact and buying time within cost limits, not achieving invincibility.
learnerActions: After iterating on the bench, discuss with someone in the role of a structural/earthquake engineer why tall buildings are allowed to sway, why base isolation works, and how real cities weigh cost against safety.
Pose and answer 'reduce, not eliminate' questions: what does each feature buy, and why can no realistic building be made fully hazard-proof?
Explain back which real trade-offs you would accept and why, connecting the bench's comparison grid to real decisions.
activities.title: Talk with an engineer: what is worth the cost?

feedback: Treat any answer that implies a building can be made fully earthquake-proof as the target misconception to address: the aim is protecting people and buying time.
Use illustrations as evocative only; do not rely on them as exact structural renderings when assessing understanding.
activities.intendedInsight: A learner can show they recognise the mechanisms, the system ordering, and the 'reduce not eliminate' idea.
learnerActions: Match each structural feature to the force or failure it counters (base isolation ↔ ground motion/inertia; cross-bracing ↔ racking; wide/low base ↔ toppling; roof damper ↔ sway).
Put the evacuation steps in order: detect → warn → act (quake detected → sea-level sensors → siren/alert → evacuate to high ground).
Given a shaking scenario, choose which redesign best meets stated criteria and set a cost/safety trade-off, explaining the reasoning.
State in your own words why the goal is reduced impact rather than a hazard-proof building.
activities.title: Consolidation checks: match mechanisms and order the chain
